name: Dusky Bluish Green
lede: Dusky Bluish Green is a dark, grayed teal first plated by Robert Ridgway in 1912, a near-twin of Dusky Blue-Green that favored Cezanne and Gauguin alike.

sections.title: A 1912 plate, with a near-twin
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* of 1912 plates this swatch at plate XXXIII, hue 41 double-prime, two hue-steps from its near-twin on the same plate, on an aged, scanned original that is itself approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS charts of 1955 file it separately at block 156, naming it a dark greenish gray, 7.2 units from this swatch [1]. The name pairs *dusky bluish* with [[green]] [1].

At hex #3D5A57 it measures lightness 36 and chroma 12 in LCH, close to gray [1]. Its closest named neighbor is [[dusky-blue-green|Dusky Blue-Green]], 2.7 units away and greener; [[invisible-green|Invisible Green]] sits 3.6 units off and almost the same color, and [[dusky-dull-green|Dusky Dull Green]] 4.0 units off and darker [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 1.37% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (326 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 126 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 63% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1300s, present in 2.0% of the 251 paintings we have from that decade (5 paintings), 3.2 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 44% of its 126 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Paul Gauguin, present in 6 of 50 works here, 6.8x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 5.0x) [3]. It is most over-represented in France, 2.2x expected (49 of 3,443 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1000, 912 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
